title: The First Breadth
passages:
The stair ended in a room with a low vault, and there the water was born. It came out of the wall at shoulder height, leaning rather than falling, a hand's width of black water sliding from a crack into a channel cut to carry it; the channel ran back down the steps they had climbed and became the river.

Ilka stepped into the channel. It was ankle-deep and cold enough to hurt. This was the first breadth, the width she had promised to cross and could no longer remember promising. Her legs remembered. They went weak under her and she put a hand on the wall to keep standing.

Above the crack, names were cut into the stone in a column, soft and rounded at the top where the oldest were, sharpening toward the floor. The lowest was fresh. She read it with her fingers before she read it with her eyes. MÁRK VASS.

Behind the stone something clicked, small and exact, a latch turning over. Ninety-five to ninety-six.

"It's stopped pulling," Márk said. He was still on the dry step with Ákos against his shoulder. "It stopped because it has me now."

"No." Ilka put both hands into the water at the mouth of the crack, and the cold went up her arms and made her teeth ache. "It has a word on a wall. It doesn't have you."

She drew breath. Márk understood half a beat too late and lunged for her, but she was already speaking, and the syllable went into the water and did not come back. "Ilka."

Nothing clicked. Then it did. Ninety-seven. Under Márk's name a new line appeared, cut wet and clean and still filling: ILKA.

Márk took her by the shoulder and turned her. His face was white. "What did you give it?"

She stood in the channel and reached for her mother's face the way she had reached for the voice and found nothing. There was a shape with the shape taken out of it, and behind the shape only the room, the water, the boy on the step. "Something with a face," she said. "I don't know yet what."

Márk knelt in the water then, boots flooding, and pressed the cord at his wrist against hers. The cold jumped between them, and for a moment she had her mother's hand on her head, the weight and warmth of it, no face and no voice but the hand, given back and not paid for. He held it there until she stopped shaking. Then he stood, lifted Ákos, and said, "The crack widens higher up. We go while it's still narrow enough to stand in."

Higher. The steps narrowed into a throat of stone. Márk carried Ákos over his shoulder, one hand under Ákos's knees, one at his belt. Ilka went before them with the cord at her wrist, though her hand stayed steady. The crack above was wider than before. It came in at the shoulder and moved. Ilka put her palm on the wall and felt the cold climb her sleeve. Márk felt the cold thread at his wrist twitch and did not look down.

"Should I carry you now?" Márk said. His voice was not joking. The river took the joke badly.

Ákos did not answer. He looked at the water. Then he said, very quietly, "Vass." His own name went into the black and did not come back. The water shuddered along the crack. Ilka turned, mouth open, and Márk saw she had lost her breath.

"No," Márk said, but Ilka was already moving toward the wall, and the cold came with her. It went under the cuff of her sleeve and up her neck. Márk made his decision then, with his body and not his voice. He lowered Ákos to the step, got him by the belt, and hauled him over the lip of the channel. Ákos was taller than the step. Márk caught him at the collar and dragged him onto the dry side, and Ákos's weight dragged Márk forward too, and then they were both on the dry side with Ákos's hands against Márk's chest and Márk's hands under Ákos's knees.

"Up," Márk said. He did not say *now* or *we* or anything with a door in it. He put Ákos over his shoulder, the way he always did, and Ilka took the cord and went before them, into the wider crack, into the water at the shoulder. Márk followed with Ákos riding high and the cold thread burning under his sleeve.

The throat let them out onto a shelf of wet stone, wide enough to lie down on, and Márk set Ákos against the wall and knelt with his palm flat on the rock. Below them the water had gone still. Not low — still, the way a held breath is still, and Ilka had no breath left to hold.

She opened her mouth to say *don't* and nothing came. She shaped the word and the air would not carry it. Márk saw her lips move, understood, and put a finger to his own.

Ákos was looking up the shelf, where the stone rose into a face of names cut deep, row on row, past the reach of the cold light. Oldest at the top, worn to shadows. Newest at the bottom, still wet. Ákos read them, and his mouth opened.

Márk got a hand over it before any sound came. "No," he said. "Not you. It comes out of her now." He tipped his head at Ilka, who stood with a hand at her throat, breathing shallow, the way a person learns to do without. "You wrote yourself, girl. Everything he says, the river bills to you."

Ilka nodded once. She had worked that out on the steps.

Then the still water moved. Not a wave — a lift, the whole surface coming up the shelf a finger's width, then another, without sound. It touched Márk's boots. The river was not pulling them down into the source. It was filling the room.

"Up," Márk said, and this time he said *we*, and the river did not take it, because it was not a name. He got Ákos over his shoulder. Ilka went first along the shelf where it climbed, and behind them the water came up the stone after them, patient, at the pace of a thing that has all night.

Behind them the water came up the next step and Márk heard it take the dry lip before he felt it. He climbed with Ákos's weight on one shoulder, the belt and collar holding, the cold thread burning under his sleeve, and Ilka went ahead of him with the cord, her breath shallow, her mouth a closed fist she held to her throat. Márk put his hand over Ákos's mouth when he felt it shape a word, though he had meant it for himself first.

They climbed until the shelf narrowed. The wall folded and the path was a ledge slick with black water, and the river was at Márk's ribs. Ákos looked up the column of names and Márk's hand went to his mouth again. Ilka read the water and went still, and her stillness was its own kind of motion.

"Up," Márk said, and it came out wrong, and he got Ákos over his shoulder anyway.

Ilka took the cord and went first. Márk followed with Ákos riding high, and behind them the water came up the ledge after them, inch by inch, and the wet names at the bottom of the column shone farther up the wall, row on row, as if the river had been reading ahead.

At the far edge of the ledge the stone dropped away. There was no higher path. Márk looked at Ilka, who could not speak and could not breathe, then at Ákos, who was silent under his hand. Márk's decision came in his arms. He lowered Ákos to the ledge, got him by the belt, and put him ahead of him on the rock. Ákos scrambled forward. Márk took his hands, and Ilka took the cord and went before him into the water, and Márk came after with Ákos riding high, and the river took the ledge and climbed after them.

The ledge ended and the shelf narrowed to a step wide enough for one boot, and Ákos went down once, hard, on the wet stone, and Márk took him back up on the belt without a word. The water came after them over the shelf with no sound at all, only the cold climbing his spine. Ilka had the cord and went first, into the place where the wall leaned in.

She stopped. Her hand went flat on the stone, and she stayed it so long that Márk turned her around by the shoulder. The rise had reached the column. At the waterline, cut fresh, the letters still beading black: ÁKOS VASS. One row above it, the same depth, the same heavy hand: SÁRA.

Márk's fingers closed on the boy's collar. Ákos read his own name in the wet and went very still, and his mouth shaped something against Márk's wrist, and Márk kept it there. Under the name the water moved, and for a breath the cut figures showed in the shine: 98. Then the rise took them and the shine went out.

Ilka tore her hand off the stone. She pointed up the column, at the next name above the water, then at herself, and shook her head; then she pointed at Márk. He felt the cold thread burn under his sleeve, and because his was the claimed wrist the river could bill without taking any memory at all, he put himself down into the rise, between the water and the names, and let it climb him while the boy and the woman went up ahead.
